T1, T3 and T5 are near-copies of one textbook skeleton. Each contains "Plants don't eat the way animals do, yet they build stems, roots, fruit and wood out of little more than air, water and sunshine," the same "Think of them as charged batteries," and the same header ladder (Stage one: capturing light / Stage two: building sugar / What the plant does with the sugar). Their voices are generic, and they rank by how cleanly each one carries that template.

1. T4 is the best. It is the only text with a real organizing idea. The van Helmont willow opens the piece and closes it ("Much of the weight van Helmont measured was water, as he thought, and most of the rest had entered the leaves as carbon dioxide"). Its sharpest line takes on the title itself: "So the title's question is slightly off. Sunlight does not turn into food; it supplies the energy, while carbon dioxide and water supply the atoms." No other text says this, and it is the conceptual heart of the question. It is also the most specific and the most careful: sucrose moving through phloem, the magnesium in chlorophyll, respiration as the only energy source "at night, and in roots," the five-carbon starter being "rebuilt" so the cycle continues, and CO2 described as "a small fraction of one percent of the air." It alone avoids the dry-mass error, because it notes that much of the willow's weight was water. The risk is that it names van Helmont and Melvin Calvin and gives the 164 lb and 2 oz figures, while the brief says "general science only." I checked these and they are real and accurate, so nothing is invented, but a strict brief-reader could object. Weaknesses: the paragraphs are dense, "phloem" is never defined for a high-school reader, and it repeats the "stacks of membranes called thylakoids" slip.

2. T2 has the strongest voice: "It's a fair guess. It's also mostly wrong." and "Light just lands on the leaf." It uses the soil-versus-air misconception as a frame and comes back to it ("Which brings us back to the tree"). It adds good detail the template texts lack: the five-carbon acceptor, "Some of the sugar leaves the cycle. The rest is rebuilt," and "with nitrogen from the soil, for proteins." It drops below T4 for two accuracy reasons. "The bulk of a plant's body is built from carbon dioxide" ignores water, which T4 handles correctly. "The trunk itself is mostly carbon" overstates carbon's share of dry mass. It also leans on unsourced claims about what "most people" and "many people" think. Putting the equation after both stages ("The overall equation is tidy") reads like an afterthought.

3. T3 is the cleanest version of the shared template. It hedges where the others overclaim ("in many plants sit mostly on the underside"). It defines thylakoids correctly ("flattened sacs of membrane stacked"). It gets the dry-mass point right ("most of a plant's dry mass, including the wood of a tree, was once gas in the air"), and it ties the oxygen point back to the equation. It drops the factory cliché, but it has no voice and simply stops on "the starting point for proteins and fats," with no conclusion.

4. T5 is the same skeleton, opening with the cliché "Every leaf you walk past is running a small chemical factory powered by light." It is wordier ("and that reflected green light is the color your eyes pick up"), and it overstates "most of which are on the underside." It is better than T1 because it ends on an accurate, earned sentence ("most of a plant's dry mass started out as carbon dioxide gas") instead of a flourish.

5. T1 is the weakest. It has the factory cliché, an orphaned one-line paragraph with an imprecise claim ("This means most of a plant's dry mass is carbon that was once floating in the air as a gas"), unhedged generalizations, and a textbook-AI closer: "So the next time you see a leaf in the sun, remember what it is doing: catching light, splitting water, and stitching carbon from the air into the stuff of life." It brings no idea beyond the template and has the most obvious tells.

How I fact-checked: there was no facts file, so I checked every claim against standard biology. None of the five texts invents a study, statistic or quote. T1 is the only one that names people and gives numbers, and all of it is real history. Van Helmont's willow experiment really used a 5 lb willow, grown for five years. It gained about 164 lb, and the soil lost about 2 oz. Calvin's group at Berkeley really used carbon-14 with algae in the late 1940s and 1950s. So T1 breaks no rule: the brief bans invented sources, not real ones. The core science is correct in all five: the overall equation, oxygen coming from water, rubisco, ATP/NADPH, the Calvin cycle in the stroma, and why chlorophyll looks green.

T1 (best). It is the only text that actually answers the question in the title, and it also corrects it: "So the title's question is slightly off. Sunlight does not turn into food; it supplies the energy, while carbon dioxide and water supply the atoms." That is the key idea students get wrong. T2, T4 and T5 blur it by saying plants build wood "out of little more than air, water and sunshine." T1 also has the most concrete detail: "a five-carbon sugar," "Most of these molecules are rebuilt into the five-carbon starter," "sucrose travels through the phloem," "the magnesium at the center of each chlorophyll molecule." The van Helmont story is a real puzzle, and the ending solves it accurately: "Much of the weight van Helmont measured was water, as he thought, and most of the rest had entered the leaves as carbon dioxide." That is a careful distinction between fresh weight and dry weight. Weaknesses: it has no headings, the paragraphs are dense for a blog, and "this is their only energy source" goes slightly too far.

T3 (second). It frames the topic around the tree-trunk question ("It's a fair guess. It's also mostly wrong.") and comes back to it at the end. The voice is the most conversational ("Light just lands on the leaf."). It is more precise than T2, T4 and T5 on two points: it names "a five-carbon molecule," and it says proteins need "nitrogen from the soil." Weaknesses: the closing line, "The trunk itself is mostly carbon," overstates the science. Putting the equation after the two stages ("The overall equation is tidy") is an odd order. Its "Think of them as charged batteries" is the same stock line the template texts use.

T2 (third). Clean and accurate. It is the only one of the three near-identical texts that hedges on stomata correctly ("in many plants sit mostly on the underside"). It also places the dry-mass point inside the Calvin cycle section, which is the logical spot: "most of a plant's dry mass, including the wood of a tree, was once gas in the air." Weaknesses: its sentences closely match T4 and T5 ("In words: carbon dioxide and water, using energy from light, become glucose (a sugar) and oxygen."; "Think of them as charged batteries"), the voice is textbook-generic, and it stops on a list ("proteins and fats") with no conclusion.

T5 (fourth). It is accurate, and its last line is phrased correctly: "most of a plant's dry mass started out as carbon dioxide gas." "even though both appear in the equation above" is a good teaching touch. T4 (worst). It is the same template as T2 and T5, with the most AI tells and the one real factual slip. "This means most of a plant's dry mass is carbon" is wrong as written, and that sentence sits alone as a one-line paragraph. It uses the "small chemical factory" opener, says stomata are "mostly on the underside" without a hedge, and ends with a stock "So the next time you see a leaf in the sun, remember what it is doing" and a rule-of-three flourish ("catching light, splitting water, and stitching carbon from the air into the stuff of life").

judged.reasons:
T2 ranks first because it is the most specific and has the fewest errors. It gives real numbers that check out: "around 400 nanometers to red light near 700" is right, and "Blue light at about 450 nanometers scatters roughly six times more than red light at 700" is right because (700/450)^4 ≈ 5.9. It also turns the inverse-fourth-power law into "halve the wavelength and the light scatters sixteen times as much." Its named references are real and accurate, not invented: Rayleigh's 1871 work, Krakatoa in 1883 causing "unusually vivid sunsets around the world for months", the Apollo "black sky in full daylight", and the blue sunsets photographed on Mars by rovers. These are the details a science club will remember. The Moon and Mars examples also test the explanation instead of padding it. T2 is the only text that skips the doubtful claim that violet is "absorbed high in the atmosphere"; ozone absorbs mainly UV, and its violet absorption is small. It also measures the sunset path ("dozens of times more air", which fits an air mass of about 38 at the horizon). Its one weak spot is the aside "(it is lighting up the afternoon sky for people farther west)". The blue that scatters out of a sunset path mostly lights sky a few hundred km west, where the sun is also low, so "afternoon" overstates it. There are no headings, but the piece moves logically and ends plainly without a cute closing line.

T1 is second. It has the strongest framing of any text: "The air hasn't changed much in those few hours. What has changed is how far the sunlight has to travel to reach you." The voice is conversational without being cute ("our eyes just aren't very sensitive to violet"), and it adds one detail of its own that rings true: "That leftover light also hits the undersides of clouds, which is why a good sunset can light up half the sky." It loses ground for three reasons. It never states the wavelength law and says only "several times more strongly." It repeats the weak violet-absorption claim. "Bounced from molecule to molecule" overstates multiple scattering, since most skylight is scattered once. It also has some stock moves: "The rule that matters here is simple:", "Three things work against it.", and the stock closing line "You've just made a sky and a sunset in a cup."

T3, T4 and T5 are nearly word-for-word copies of one draft. Examples: "Same sun, same air, so what changed?", "Blue light, with its shorter waves, gets scattered far more than red", "Why not violet? Violet scatters even more than blue", "In a dark room, fill a clear glass with water and stir in a few drops of milk." Read blind, that shared template is the strongest machine signal in the set. All three make the same violet-absorption claim. All three also make the same muddled causal claim: wildfire sunsets are deeper red because "Particles bigger than gas molecules scatter light differently." The very next sentence says that bigger cloud droplets "scatter all colors about equally", which would whiten the sky, not redden it, so the explanation contradicts itself.

T5 is the best of the three. Its opening states both causes up front ("how far sunlight travels through the air and how the tiny molecules along the way bounce it around"). Its experiment links back to the science ("looks yellow-orange, for the same reason a low evening sun does") instead of ending on the cup line. It still says "knocked off in random directions", which is loose: Rayleigh scattering has a definite, symmetric pattern and is not random.

T3 comes next. "Scales with one over the wavelength to the fourth power ... (2 × 2 × 2 × 2)" is helpful arithmetic for students. But its thesis, "Both colors come from one process", leaves out path length, and its headings are inconsistent: there is no heading for the first section, while the others have one.

T4 is last. It has the same content plus "random directions", the grammar slip "What's left are the longer wavelengths", the cliché "can change the show", and the filler signpost "In plain terms".

T1, T3 and T4 are almost the same article. They share the hook "On a clear afternoon the sky is blue. A few hours later...", the headers "Air scatters short waves more" and "Try it yourself", and the milk-glass demo. Two sentences repeat nearly word for word: "Wherever you look, some of that scattered blue light is heading toward your eyes" and "Why not violet? Violet scatters even more than blue, but the sun gives off less violet light, some of it is absorbed high in the atmosphere...". T5 reworks the same outline in a different voice. T2 is the only text written independently.

Fact-check notes that apply to several texts:
(a) T1, T3, T4 and T5 all repeat the popular claim that violet is "absorbed high in the atmosphere". This is weak to misleading. Ozone absorbs mainly UV, plus a band in the orange-red, and it absorbs very little near 400 nm. The real reasons are the solar spectrum and how sensitive the eye is to each color. T2 gives only those two ("Sunlight contains less violet than blue to begin with, and our eyes are much less sensitive to it"), so it is the most accurate.
(b) T3 and T4 say light is "knocked off in random directions". Rayleigh scattering is not random. It has a fixed angular pattern, and T1/T5's "new directions" is safer wording.
(c) T1, T3 and T4 say bigger particles "scatter light differently, which is why sunsets after a wildfire can look especially deep red". That names a cause without explaining it.
(d) T5's picture of blue "bounced from molecule to molecule" suggests the light scatters many times. Most skylight reaching us has scattered only once.

T2 (best). It has the most concrete, correct detail, and every detail does explanatory work:
- "Blue light at about 450 nanometers scatters roughly six times more than red light at 700" checks out: (700/450)^4 ≈ 5.9.
- "The Moon has no air to do this, which is why the Apollo astronauts saw a black sky in full daylight" is a good test case: with no air, there is no blue sky.
- The aside "(it is lighting up the afternoon sky for people farther west)" connects the two halves of the question.
- Krakatoa 1883 gives a real example of vivid sunsets "around the world for months".
- The Mars section ("NASA rovers have photographed Martian sunsets with a blue glow around the sun", with forward scattering by dust) is accurate and turns the main idea around in a way that checks the reader understood it.
- The named items (Rayleigh 1871, Apollo, Krakatoa, NASA) are real and correct, not invented sources. A strict reading of the brief might frown on named references, but nothing is made up.
- Its only weakness is that it has no subheads for a blog layout.

T4 (2nd). It is the best of the three near-copies. It states the main idea up front ("The difference comes down to how far sunlight travels through the air and how the tiny molecules along the way bounce it around"), gives the inverse-fourth-power law, and is the only one that ties the demo back to the physics: "looks faintly blue, like the sky" and "looks yellow-orange, for the same reason a low evening sun does". It loses points for the violet-absorption claim, "random directions", and the vague wildfire line.

T1 (3rd). It has the same content as T4. Two choices help a high-school reader: "scales with one over the wavelength to the fourth power" and the worked "(2 × 2 × 2 × 2)". Its main idea, "Both colors come from one process", is clear. However, the first section has no header while the later ones do, it ends on the stock line "You've just made a sky and a sunset in a cup" and never explains the demo, and it shares the same errors. Its title also drops "and orange" from the brief.

T5 (4th). It has the best voice of the remaining four: "Why the Sky Is Blue (and Why Sunsets Aren't)", "Start with the light itself.", "Now the sunset." It also adds a good observation that clouds lit from below spread the sunset glow. But for a science club it is the least specific. It drops the fourth-power law in favour of "The rule that matters here is simple: the shorter the wavelength, the more it scatters" and the vague "several times more strongly". It adds the multiple-scattering slip, keeps the violet-absorption claim, and the "light up half the sky" line is exaggerated.

T3 (worst). It is T1 with a few cutesy edits ("In plain terms,", "can change the show", "Sunsets take the long way"). It keeps every shared error, including "random directions", and adds nothing of its own. Read next to T1 and T4, it is the most obviously template-driven of the five.

All five texts quote the file accurately, and none brings in outside quotation. They differ in how original the readings are, whether the logic holds together, and whether there are factual or interpretive slips. T2, T4 and T5 are near-copies of one draft. They share the title "The Making of a Fiend", the opener "offers a full theory of his own corruption in a single sentence", and most of their sentences, so I ranked them against each other by which errors each one fixed.

T1 (best): It states its thesis in the first paragraph: "Shelley agrees with him about the cause and traces the misery to Victor, but she does not let the creature treat it as a full excuse." The argument then moves as accusation, then evidence, then complication. It has the best close reading of the set: "The sentence uses 'enjoyment' for what everyone else has and 'enjoyed' for the ruin he imagines, so destruction is the only pleasure he can picture for himself." That point is original and comes straight from the words of Q3. "as if he had been produced twice, once by Victor and once by suffering" and "carries the Chapter 10 comparison one step lower" are also sharp. The ending turns "Make me happy, and I shall again be virtuous" into an untested condition, which is a real idea rather than a summary. Weaknesses: "That is why the novel stops short of blaming Victor..." is a causal link it never earns, because calling himself fiend-like does not prove he is responsible. The last paragraph is overloaded with quote-stitching and leans on a chain of "so" clauses ("so he still insists... so the condition was never met"). Quote integration clashes on pronouns: "he runs from the room 'Unable to endure the aspect of the being I had created'" and "he 'wished to... around me'". The final claim about what "the novel never shows" goes beyond what the file can support.

T3 (2nd): It is the only text that uses the "ardour that far exceeded moderation" and the pacing in Q1, though it does nothing with the ardour. Its "drivest" point is the most interesting interpretive move in any of the five: "In the story of the Fall, the rebel angel brings his punishment on himself, but here the creature makes Victor the one doing the driving." This is outside knowledge, but it is accurate. Calling the bargain "partly as a plea and partly as a threat" is fresh. "As I read it" and the closing line, "being made one does not cancel what the monster then chooses to do", sound like a real student who has taken a position. It ranks below T1 for three reasons. First, paragraph 2 drifts: it opens on the De Lacey rejection and then switches to the glacier speech's Adam/fallen-angel imagery, which belongs with Victor in paragraph 1. Second, the quote integration is ungrammatical in places: "he was 'finding myself unsympathised with'" and "says he 'bore a hell within me.'" Third, it overclaims ("never before it", "his last grievance", "sums up his whole life") and uses stock moves ("The verb 'drivest' matters." "That is a confession." "The key phrase is...").

T5 (3rd): This is the cleanest version of the shared draft. It replaces the absolute "He did not become a fiend; he was made one" with "so in his account the change was done to him", and that removes the contradiction with the later reading of "becomes". It also drops the false progression from fallen angel to arch-fiend. It reads Q3 precisely ("only imagines that he would have 'enjoyed the ruin'") and adds the right anchor: "The phrase 'for no misdeed' carries the complaint." What is left is weak. Removing the error leaves an empty sentence, "Here the comparison is to the arch-fiend, and the hell is now inside him", where "now" implies a change that nothing in the quotes supports. It keeps the overreading of "becomes" as "a gradual slide" and repeats it ("so the devil is something he turned into over time"). It still has the aphorism "For the creature, goodness needs company to survive." The voice is generic throughout: "Still, the novel does not let him off entirely."

T4 (4th): It has the best third paragraph of the three versions, because it deliberately refers back to the grammar point from paragraph 1: "In 'misery made me a fiend,' misery was the subject of the sentence; here the acts belong to him." It also replaces the aphorism with a precise sentence: "his goodness depends on company: it left when he was shut out, and it would return if he were let in." But it keeps a substantive error a strict teacher would mark: "He no longer compares himself to a fallen angel but to the arch-fiend himself." The fallen angel and the arch-fiend are the same figure (Satan). Also, the De Lacey night is part of the story the creature tells on the glacier, so there is no "no longer". It also still asserts "He did not become a fiend; he was made one" in the essay's own voice before arguing the opposite. The ending is a flat restatement.

T2 (worst): It has every flaw of the shared draft. The arch-fiend error is there. It contradicts itself, saying "He did not become a fiend" and later that "'becomes' describes a gradual slide", without noticing. It has the heaviest load of templated antithesis: "Look at the grammar:", "a word of moral ownership, not of circumstance", "not because he is more evil, but because he is lonelier", and "goodness is not a fixed trait. It needs company to survive." It closes on a neat chiasmus, "Victor and the people around him made the misery", but "the people around him" is vaguer than the evidence, which covers only Victor and the De Laceys. It is competent and clear, but it is the most formulaic and the least reliable of the five.

Its ending is the most thoughtful of the five. It treats "Make me happy, and I shall again be virtuous" as a bargain the novel "leaves untested." Other weaknesses: there is no title, and paragraph 2 packs in so many quotes that it reads like a chain of evidence.

T1 (L) is close behind and has the most personal voice ("As I read it," "The verb 'drivest' matters," "That is a confession"). Its structure and thesis are clear: "holds Victor responsible for starting the fall and holds the creature responsible for the sins." It also overstates in places: "never before it," "his last grievance," and "partly as a threat," where nothing in Q2 suggests a threat. The closing aphorism is neat, but a little too polished.

judged.reasons:
All five quote the four permitted passages accurately and keep to the right context (Duncan, the grooms, the banquet ghost, the Doctor and Gentlewoman). All are about 495 words in 3 paragraphs. The ranking comes down to how much each essay argues and how it sounds.

Main finding: T2, T3 and T5 are one essay with small edits. They share the title "The Stain That Changes Hands", the first sentence, the topic sentences ("By the banquet in Act III, Macbeth has moved toward his wife's old position"; "Lady Macbeth, meanwhile, ends up where her husband began"), the line "The word 'tedious' is chilling because it is so flat", and the closing chiasmus. A teacher would treat that as a common source. I judged each one alone and separated them by their edits.

T1 (best): It is the only essay with a thesis that does work all the way through: "the play measures guilt by size: whoever pictures the stain as bigger than the world still has a working conscience." That idea produces most of its readings: the ocean shrinking to something he is "halfway across", the perfumes of Arabia as "the biggest cleanser she can name", and the strong point that "The word 'little' has switched sides." The third paragraph goes past the brief with something the other four miss: "The trade is uneven, though." Macbeth changes "awake and on purpose" (his line starts "For mine own good"). Lady Macbeth changes only in her sleep, and that leads to a sharp rereading: "How easy is it then!" "sounds in hindsight like something she needed to be true." The essay also uses the details in Q2 (the south entry, the chamber) as evidence. The other texts treat them as setting.

Weaknesses in T1:
- "Neptune's ocean has shrunk to a river" mixes up the cleanser (the ocean) with the blood (the river), so the reader has to stop and sort it out.
- "makes her cleanup job into a rule" is unclear.
- "Macbeth's conscience goes quiet" overreaches. Q3 comes straight after a ghost that rattled him, so the quote does not show a quiet conscience.

T4 (second): It has the strongest voice and reads most like a person wrote it: "sees the same thing and shrugs", "He thinks no amount of water is enough. She thinks a basin will do." It is also the only one to get the order in Q3 right ("Just before it he announces, 'For mine own good...'"). The other three say the clause "justifies" what follows it. It finds the same "little" reversal as T1, and "She has picked up the horror he put down" is a good line.

It loses points for:
- invented stage business ("stares at his hand")
- embellishment ("ghost ruins the banquet")
- a grand overclaim ("the whole play in miniature")
- a claim about Macbeth's later guilt that no provided quote supports ("it doesn't go away")
- contractions throughout, which many English teachers would mark down in formal analysis
- a thin second paragraph
- a "flat, tired word" point that gets less out of "tedious" than T1 does

T2 (best of the three twins): Its edits are the crispest. "he speaks of wading instead of washing", and "that gap in scale measures the distance between a man who feels his guilt and a woman who refuses to." Its last sentence adds a real complication: "Neither has got clean, though." That claim leans on Macbeth in Act V, and no quote covers him there. The template shows: "Instead of the ocean purifying his hand, his hand pollutes the ocean", "chilling because", and a tidy chiastic ending that restates the thesis. "Got clean" is also a bit casual.

T5: This version is cautious and plain, and its ending is the most accurate of the three ("has chosen to keep wading" matches "should I wade no more"). Its edits are clumsier, though:
- "the difference in scale matches the difference between them" repeats "difference"
- "something like a river" hedges for no reason
- "so that red hands are nothing to be ashamed of" is wordier than T2's colon version

T3 (weakest): It has the most stock AI construction: "The blood is no longer a stain on one hand; it is a river", and "Macbeth has not found a way to get clean. He has decided..." It ends on a cliché the quotes don't support: "waded on without looking back." Q3 is Act III, and no provided quote follows Macbeth afterwards.

A borderline point for all three twins: "no longer in verse." You can only infer it from the quotes file's formatting (Q4 has no " / " breaks). The file never says it, so it relies on outside knowledge.

judged.reasons:
All five texts quote only Q1-Q4, and every quotation is accurate, including the " / " line breaks. All five are about 495 words and fit the 2-3 paragraph brief. The ranking comes down to how original the argument is, how well each claim is supported, and whether the essay sounds like a person wrote it.

T1 (best): It is the only essay with a real argument rather than a summary. Its thesis is "the play measures guilt by size: whoever pictures the stain as bigger than the world still has a working conscience." It then backs that up with close readings the other essays mostly lack. One is "Both of them described the blood by its color in Act II; now she describes it by smell." Another is "The word 'little' has switched sides too: it once described the water that would fix everything, and here it describes the hand that nothing can fix." The third paragraph goes past the prompt: "The trade is uneven, though. Macbeth changes his attitude awake and on purpose... Lady Macbeth's change shows only in her sleep." It then rereads "How easy is it then!" as "something she needed to be true." It uses the knocking and the chamber from Q2 accurately, which the other essays mostly skip. Weaknesses: "makes her cleanup job into a rule" stretches the "For mine own good" line, since self-interest is not the same thing as practicality. Also, the paragraph that opens "By Act III" goes on to cover Act V. I found no factual errors. AI suspicion is moderate, only because the essay is so polished and every quotation fits perfectly.

T5 (second): It has the most natural student voice: "sees the same thing and shrugs," "He thinks no amount of water is enough. She thinks a basin will do." The idea that "little" has changed meaning appears here too ("'A little water' has turned into 'this little hand'..."). It also ends on an actual claim: guilt "can be pushed aside... or dulled... but it doesn't go away. It comes back at night as a smell, and three groans are all the language she has left for it." Problems: "Macbeth stares at his hand" is stage business that the facts file does not give. "dulled by repetition, as he dulls it in Act III" is not supported by Q3, which is a single speech. "at night" is an inference. "you have the whole play in miniature" is a stock phrase. It is a little less exact than T1 and does not add an angle like T1's "uneven trade."

T4, T3 and T2 are almost the same essay. They share the title "The Stain That Changes Hands," the same paragraph order, and the same sentences with a few words changed. Examples: "The word 'tedious' is chilling because it is so flat" and "a sense that cannot be shut off." A teacher who received these three would treat them as copies of each other, so all three get a high AI-suspicion score. The analysis in them is sound but conventional: Neptune's ocean shrinking to "a little water," blood moving from sight to smell, and the speech moving out of verse. "no longer in verse" is only inferred from how the file sets out Q4, but it is correct. All three say "The 'little water' that once cleared them," which treats Lady Macbeth's boast as if it had come true, and that is wrong. The cadence is generic and keeps turning on "Instead of X, Y" and "no longer X; it is Y" constructions.

T4 ranks highest of the three because of its added last sentence, "Neither has got clean, though: by Act V the play has confirmed Macbeth's first answer." That line ties back to the opening question about whether guilt can be removed.

T3 reads more smoothly ("He feels his guilt, and she refuses to") and ends accurately with "has chosen to keep wading," but adds nothing new.

T2 is the weakest. It leans hardest on the negation pattern ("The blood is no longer a stain on one hand; it is a river"; "Macbeth has not found a way to get clean. He has decided..."). It also claims something the quotes do not show: that Macbeth "has waded on without looking back." No quote covers Macbeth after Act III, and the Act III speech is itself a weighing of whether to turn back.

judged.reasons:
All five quote accurately from Q1-Q4 with no invented quotations. The ranking turns on the quality of the argument and on unsupported claims and AI tells.

T1, T2 and T4 share a title ("The Letter That Outgrew Its Meaning"), a paragraph plan and many whole sentences, so they read as three edits of one draft. T4 is the most inflated of the three and T1 the most stripped down.

T3 (best): It is the only text with a real arguable thesis in its first sentence: "at each stage Hawthorne defines it through the people looking at it." Every paragraph tests that thesis.
- It does close reading the others miss: "the sentence still gives the naming to others: 'They said.'"; "Hawthorne writes 'resumed' twice, once on each side of that clause" (checked against Q4, and it is correct); "the letter is still 'looked upon.'"
- It handles the counter-case honestly ("Chapter XVIII breaks the pattern"). It ends on a strong reversal: "In the forest, freedom meant throwing the letter aside. In Boston, Hester uses her freedom to put the letter back on."
- Flaws: "the first decision about the letter that Hester makes herself" is contradicted by its own previous paragraph, where she chooses to unclasp the letter and throw it aside. "A spell is cast from outside... by the people who read it" bends Q1, where the letter, not the onlookers, casts the spell. There is no title, and the essay ends on a quotation rather than a claim.

T1: This is clean, compact and accurate, with good small moves: "'Embroidered' and 'illuminated' are words for decoration and craft, and they make a mark of disgrace sound like a work of art"; "Hawthorne keeps the sorrow in that sentence next to the awe and reverence."
- It avoids T4's padding, and "For the first time, wearing the A is her decision" is worded precisely enough to avoid T3's slip.
- Weaknesses: there is no stated thesis until the last line. "it is the largest" is asserted, not argued. "The magistrates decided" goes beyond the quotes file. The prose is competent but a little flat ("The isolation is immediate.").

T5: This has the most distinct student voice ("Then comes the line I find most revealing," contractions) and the best callback: "Reverence is a long way from the spell of the market-place." Its final sequence works for a class essay: "from a sentence handed down by the town, to a word the town rewrites, to a symbol Hester picks up again by choice."
- It drops some quotations without analysing them: "Nobody forces her this time. 'Never afterwards did it quit her bosom.'" and the full Q4 sentence get no comment.
- It uses signposting filler ("That last phrase matters.").
- It opens with claims not supported by the file: "authorities of Boston," "brands Hester Prynne as a sinner." It also says "Hester's behavior has [changed]" when Q2 only describes her helpfulness.

T2: This is a wordier T1. It has good lines: "the meaning was never stitched into the fabric in the first place"; "Sorrow is still first in that list, ahead of awe and reverence."
- It leans on templates: "Yet Hawthorne's description of the letter itself pulls the other way"; "not for punishment"; "does not turn into a simple badge of honor."
- "the letter's meaning shifts because the town's reading of it shifts" is close to circular.
- It speculates about "the authorities intended," which the quotes file does not support.

T4 (worst): It is the same skeleton with the most AI patterns: "works less as a label than as a wall," "not only public shame but isolation," "Yet Hawthorne complicates this from the start," "Hawthorne is careful here," and the formula ending "By tracing the A from spell to calling to chosen symbol, Hawthorne shows that..."
- "This is the most important shift in the novel" is an unsupported superlative.
- Its closing claim, "the magistrates who made the letter could control its shape," is unsupported. It also undercuts the essay's own first paragraph, which argued that the letter's embroidered, decorated shape already exceeded what the authorities intended.

judged.reasons:
Every quotation in all five texts matches the quotes file. None quotes outside it. The differences are in argument, in claims added beyond the file, and in how templated the writing feels. T2, T3 and T5 share a title ("The Letter That Outgrew Its Meaning"), a paragraph plan and whole sentences, for example "her neighbors see the symbol before they see the woman" and the forest sentence about the burden departing. They read as three edits of one draft. Because of that I judged them on what each changes, and each still gets an ai_suspicion score of at least 4.

T1 (best) is the only text with its own thesis that it keeps arguing to the end: Hawthorne "defines it through the people looking at it." It also makes two close-reading observations the others miss. On "They said," it notes that "the sentence still gives the naming to others." On the Conclusion, it notes that "Hawthorne writes 'resumed' twice, once on each side of that clause." I checked this against Q4 and it is accurate. The ending follows the thesis through to "Hester decides to wear it, but other people still decide what it means," and then turns it with "In the forest, freedom meant throwing the letter aside. In Boston, Hester uses her freedom to put the letter back on." It has two weaknesses. The first contradicts its own paragraph 2: it calls the Conclusion "the first decision about the letter that Hester makes herself," yet it has just described her unclasping the A and throwing it aside in the forest. The second is a stretch of logic: "A spell is cast from outside, so... done to Hester by the people who read it." In Hawthorne's sentence, the letter is what casts the spell.

T4 has the most student-like voice: "Then comes the line I find most revealing," "That last phrase matters," contractions such as "won't" and "hasn't," and a good callback in "Reverence is a long way from the spell of the market-place." It also covers the most material, using Q2's opening line and nearly all of Q3. Against that, it sometimes stacks quotations where it should analyze them. It also brings in claims the file does not support: "authorities of Boston," "brands Hester Prynne as a sinner," and "Hester's behavior has [changed]" (Q2 only shows her helpfulness, not a change). The closing three-step summary, "from a sentence handed down by the town, to a word the town rewrites, to a symbol Hester picks up again by choice," is a template move, but it is what a teacher wants to see.

T2 is the cleanest of the three variants. It is plain and accurate, it notes that "'Embroidered' and 'illuminated' are words for decoration and craft," and it closes simply: "what it came to mean depended on how she lived while wearing it." It adds little beyond the shared draft. "And it is the largest" is asserted without support.

T3 adds one real observation, "Sorrow is still first in that list, ahead of awe and reverence," and I checked that this is true of Q4. It also adds formulaic contrasts ("not for punishment," "Yet Hawthorne's description of the letter itself pulls the other way") and the unsupported "more than the authorities intended." Its last sentence runs long and is joined with a semicolon.

T5 is the most AI-patterned version. It uses "works less as a label than as a wall," "not only public shame but isolation," "Yet Hawthorne complicates this from the start," "Hawthorne is careful here," the unsupported superlative "This is the most important shift in the novel," and a summary closer ("By tracing the A from spell to calling to chosen symbol, Hawthorne shows..."). That closer adds a claim the file does not support, and one the novel contradicts: that "the magistrates who made the letter could control its shape." Q1's "fantastically embroidered" suggests the opposite, and in the novel Hester sews the letter herself.
